column4: The answer to Thamud's accusation says that tomorrow they will know who is the insolent liar; this ayah reverses the charge in 54:25 before the camel trial begins.
Salih says that he asks no payment for his message, supplying a concrete reason to obey the trustworthy messenger rather than the people's self-interested chiefs.
Thamud call Salih one of the bewitched immediately before objecting that he is only human; this ayah contributes their first counterword to the messenger's command.
Salih asks why his people hasten evil before good and urges them to seek forgiveness; it supplies the messenger's warning to which their evil-omen accusation in 27:47 replies.
The universal Messenger commands belief in God and His messenger and says to follow him so that the hearers may be guided, directly naming the rightful following-line.
Noah's elite reject a human like themselves, accuse him of seeking superiority, and claim that God would have sent angels; their argument closely matches Thamud's refusal to follow one human.
The chiefs call the human messenger a possessed man and tell the people to wait him out, completing the accusatory speech begun in 23:24.
The elite describe their messenger as a mortal who eats and drinks like the people; this is the premise for their warning in 23:34 against obeying a human like themselves.
Opponents ask what sort of messenger eats food and walks in markets, another specific rejection of a human bearer on the basis of shared humanity.
God answers that earlier messengers also ate food and walked in markets and made people a trial for one another; ordinary humanity is part of the sending, not a reason to reject it.
The opponents demand that an angel be sent down with the human messenger, restating the false assumption that a human bearer is insufficient.
God says that even an angelic messenger would be made to appear as a man, exposing why the human-form objection cannot identify a false commission.
A believing man from Pharaoh's household stands up to defend Moses because he says "My Lord is God" and has brought proofs; his initiative reverses the worst man's leadership in Thamud.
The believing man says "follow me; I will guide you to the way of right conduct," making a righteous self-mobilized human voice the opposite of a chief who guides his people to ruin.
The believer sets the two calls side by side: he calls his people to salvation while they call him to the Fire, exactly articulating opposed following-lines.
He explains that they call him to disbelief while he calls them to the Mighty, Forgiving God; this ayah supplies the contents and destinations of the rival invitations.
A person disputes about God without knowledge and follows every rebellious devil, identifying a destructive speaker with the leader he follows.
It is decreed that whoever takes that rebellious devil as guide will be led astray and guided to the Blaze, a direct leader-follower-result sequence.
God's covenant forbids serving Satan because he is a manifest enemy, establishing the prohibition before naming the multitudes he led astray.
The command to worship God is identified as the straight path, supplying the rightful course opposite Satan's following-line.
Satan has led a great multitude astray; the hearers are asked why they did not reason, exposing the scale of following as no defense for its direction.
Failure to answer the messenger reveals that the opponents follow their desires, and the ayah asks who is more astray than one who follows desire without divine guidance.
The People of the Book are forbidden to follow the desires of a people who went astray, led many astray, and strayed from the level way; leaders and followers share the deviation.
Satan tells his followers that he merely called and they responded, then disowns their attempt to blame him; the speech lays bare agency within a ruinous following-line.
Like Pharaoh's people before them, deniers are destroyed بِذُنُوبِهِمْ; the shared wording joins collective denial, destructive leadership, and the ordinary "sins" sense of the source section's ذنب.
The verse explicitly includes Thamud among peoples whose messengers brought proofs and who replied that they disbelieved in what the messengers were sent with.
Whenever a warner is sent to a town, its affluent leaders declare disbelief in the message, generalizing the role played by Thamud's leading group.
Earlier peoples deny messengers even though their bearers bring clear proofs, scriptures, and the illuminating Book, joining the carrier to the carried word.
God then seizes those who disbelieve; this ayah supplies the result of the messenger-denial scene stated in 35:25.
God sent messengers among the communities of earlier peoples, establishing the repeated historical setting for the next ayah's response.
No messenger came without being mocked, giving the recurrent rejection enacted specifically by Thamud's taunts to Salih.
Messengers before Muhammad were mocked, and the very warning mocked came to surround the mockers; rejection and outcome turn back upon the speakers.
Moses asks why his people harm him although they know he is God's messenger; when they deviate, their hearts are made to deviate, linking treatment of the messenger to direction.
Jesus identifies himself as God's messenger, confirms the preceding scripture, and announces a later messenger; when clear proofs arrive, the hearers dismiss them as magic.
At Hell's gates the keepers ask whether messengers from among the condemned recited God's signs and warned them; the answer admits the warning and its realized result.
Whoever obeys the Messenger obeys God, grounding the messenger's claim to be followed in the Sender rather than in personal rank.
Believers are told to answer God and the Messenger when the Messenger calls them to what gives life, the life-giving opposite of answering a chief who leads to destruction.
Once God and His Messenger decide a matter, believers have no competing choice; disobedience is named clear error, fixing the authority of the sent bearer over rival human preference.
Those who mislead others carry their own full burdens and some burdens of people led without knowledge, showing how a leader's offense extends through the followers he recruits.
The leaders admit that they led the others astray because they themselves were astray, an explicit confession of the destructive line represented by Thamud's worst man.
Leaders and followers share the punishment, giving the consequence of the admitted misguidance in 37:32.
People command righteousness while forgetting themselves although they recite the Scripture; this is the boundary between tilawa as mere reading and tilawa embodied by tracing the Book.
Jesus says God did not make him a domineering wretch, جَبَّارًا شَقِيًّا; a divinely commissioned speaker is expressly separated from the wretched tyrant type that people wrongly follow.

The sleepers deliberately send one of their own to the city with money and instructions for care; this benign group commission contrasts with Thamud's uncommissioned worst man and the companion summoned to offend.
The moon is darkened before sun and moon are joined in 75:9, beginning the end-time reversal of the luminous, ordered following seen in the section.
Salih's opening question, asking whether Thamud will be mindful, initiates the messenger's direct address before he identifies himself in 26:143.
The Messenger is told to say that love of God is shown by following him, giving a positive personal form of following the divinely sent human bearer.
The next command requires obedience to God and the Messenger and marks turning away as disbelief, supplying the negative boundary to 3:31.
Believers are told to obey God and His Messenger and not turn away while hearing, joining reception of the spoken word to enacted obedience.
The Messenger identifies his way as calling to God with insight, both for himself and whoever follows him; followers continue the same informed call rather than a chief's blind line.
The Messenger's responsibility is only clear delivery, distinguishing faithful carriage of the message from the hearers' responsibility for their response.
God sends messengers with clear proofs and sends down the Book and balance so people may uphold justice; the dispatched bearers carry a word intended to shape conduct.
The command to recite what has been revealed is followed by prayer's restraint from wrong, linking the spoken tilawa of scripture to an embodied moral trace.
When God's signs are recited, opponents claim they could produce the same and call them old tales; their counter-speech is another form of assigning falsehood to the carried word.
One who hears God's signs recited yet persists arrogantly as though unheard receives a painful warning, connecting recitation, refusal, and outcome.
Those charged with the Torah but failing to bear it are likened to a donkey carrying books; the image distinguishes possession of revelation from living in its trace.
Every messenger is sent in the language of his people so that he can make the message clear, tying divine dispatch to intelligible human speech.
Messengers bring good news and warning so people have no argument after them; the ayah defines how a delivered message precedes judgment.
Those classed as wretched in 11:105 are in the Fire here, giving the destination of the source section's شقاوة term.
Night is wrapped over day and day over night while sun and moon each run to a stated term, giving another measured celestial succession.
God makes night enter day and day enter night and subjects sun and moon, each running to a fixed term; ordered alternation frames the same celestial pair.
The same joining of night and day and appointed courses of sun and moon repeats the rule-governed cosmic line against which human following is measured.
Sun and moon are subjected and each runs for an appointed term, locating their movement under divine direction rather than self-assertion.
God subjects the sun and moon as two beings continually running their courses, reinforcing the regular service implicit in the moon's following.
Night is made for rest and sun and moon for reckoning; their measured function connects celestial order to human recognition.
Wrongdoers have a ذَنُوبًا, an allotted share like that of their companions; this distinct Quranic sense of the source section's ذنب root makes shared consequence itself the followers' portion.
Believers are forbidden to put themselves ahead of God and His Messenger, a positional rule that prevents a human will from taking the head of the revelatory line.
Thamud are explicitly included among earlier peoples who denied, placing their response within the repeated history of communities rejecting warning.
